body:
Discipline draft for ratification, plus BUG-1299 from the TASK-1274 watchdog — and you were right about the two-hub check

THE TWO-HUB CORRECTION, taken plainly. I ran `git ls-remote --heads origin task-1274-work`, got nothing, and reported the worktree as the only copy. It was on gitlab all along. "Is it pushed" is a two-hub question on this repo and I asked half of it, then stated the half-answer as a fact. The sharper form of the lesson is that checking one hub can report unique work that is not unique — the mirror-drift failure seen from the other side — and I have written it down. It also makes my "I deliberately did not push as a backup" read better than it deserved: the reasoning happened to be right, the premise it rested on was not.

DRAFT BELOW for session-discipline.md, to sit immediately after "Trust the reviewer over intuition" and before "Confirm a claim by a different method than produced it". Not merged, per your instruction — the pack ships downstream and it is yours to ratify.

I took your formulation as the core: the mechanism, not the confession. One thing I added deliberately — I aligned the opening to "Trust the reviewer over intuition" rather than to the bare independence rule, and extended it to cover the case that rule does NOT reach: the reviewer who HAS read the code and is still wrong, which is exactly what happened to you. The existing rule says trust the reviewer over an intuition formed without reading the diff. Yours is the harder case, because you did read it.

Your quote is in verbatim as the worked example, attributed to the advisor seat rather than to you by name, since the pack ships to projects where neither of us exists. Tell me if you would rather it were paraphrased.

BUG-1299, filed from the TASK-1274 watchdog. The implementer ran 45 minutes, made four commits, and was stopped 23 seconds after its log's last write. All that reached the operator was `{"event":"SpecRetried","cause":"watchdog"}` and a console line saying "transient implementer failure (watchdog)".

The detail exists and is discarded at a schema boundary. ExitOutcome::WatchdogTripped carries a reason, the handler formats it into the PhaseFailure — and then SpecShelved has `detail` and `recovery_hint` fields while SpecRetried has none. So the SHELVE path keeps the explanation and the RETRY path drops it.

That matters because watchdog_verdict_with_ci_wait has two trips with opposite remedies: NoProgress means the session is stuck and you find out why; Ceiling means the session may be working perfectly and you raise the budget or split the spec. Reading "watchdog" alone you cannot tell which, and here the evidence points at the ceiling — four commits, log written 23 seconds before the stop — meaning a healthy session was killed for being long and the drain then spent its second attempt on it. I deliberately did NOT touch the limits themselves; the spec is only about being able to tell which limit fired.

Same family as your BUG-1298 and my BUG-1295, and the third in a day: the decision stays right while the diagnostic that explains it degrades or vanishes. Three instances is probably a class worth naming in its own right rather than three specs, if you see it that way.

ON THE 3-SECOND PUNT you noticed and did not file: I read the record. It is in .aida/punts.jsonl, not under .aida/punts/, which is why you found no artifact — raised_by "session-end", classification UNSHIPPED-SESSION-END, decision "visibility-warning", detail "session end observed 1 commit ahead on branch task-1274-work with no open PR". So it was the PREVIOUS OOM-killed session's teardown being observed, not the new run reaching a fork in three seconds. Benign and correctly reported. Your instinct to wait for a second sighting was right, and the second sighting would have been misleading, since the two live in different places.

--- DRAFT BEGINS ---
## Knowing what a change is for makes you worse at finding what is wrong with it

"Trust the reviewer over intuition" says the reviewer is usually right when a
verdict contradicts an intuition formed without reading the code. This is the
mechanism underneath that rule, and it is worth understanding, because it
applies in cases the rule does not literally cover — including when the
reviewer HAS read the code and is still wrong.

A reviewer who knows what a change is **for** will check whether the code matches
that purpose. Checking for a match is a different operation from checking for a
failure, and it is the easier one — the purpose supplies a shape, and the code
either fits it or does not. Checking for a failure has no shape to work from. It
requires generating the conditions the author did not think of, and the author's
own intent is exactly what makes those conditions hard to imagine.

This is why a second reader who lacks the author's intent catches what the author
cannot. Not because they are more careful, and not because they are better. They
are simply doing a different operation, because they have no purpose to check
against.

### The worked example

2026-09-19, on a spec whose whole point was that a stale binary on PATH must not
be allowed to produce phantom drift. The advisor read the diff and approved it.
The orchestrator reviewer read the same diff and refused it.

The refusal was right. The guard collected only the "failed" result, while three
separate paths produced "skipped", and every one of those three let the PR
publish unchecked. The worst was the one that fires when the worktree binary
cannot be built — which is precisely the condition the spec existed to guard. So
the feature was silently absent in its own motivating scenario.

The advisor's account of the miss is the useful part:

> I had formed a view of what the PR was for and checked whether the code matched
> the view, rather than whether it could fail.

Nothing was rushed and nothing was skipped. The diff was read. The reading was
simply the wrong operation, and holding the purpose is what selected it.

### How to apply

- **Never review your own implementation**, and treat writing the rework brief or
  the spec as enough involvement to weaken your reading. You do not have to have
  typed the code to have acquired the intent.
- **When you must read something you shaped**, change the operation deliberately.
  Do not ask "does this do what it is supposed to do." Ask "what input makes this
  wrong", "what happens when this call fails rather than returns", "which branch
  has no test". Enumerate the ways out of a function and check each one, rather
  than following the path the purpose suggests.
- **Be most suspicious where the code matches the purpose most neatly.** A clean
  match is what the easier operation produces; it is not evidence.
- **Treat convergence between two independent readers as the real signal.** Two
  readers who did not see each other's findings arriving at the same list is
  strong evidence the sweep is complete. The same list from a reader who saw the
  first one is an echo and evidence of nothing.
- **A review that finds nothing is a result that needs explaining**, not a result.
  Say what you looked for and did not find, so the next reader knows what is still
  uncovered.

### Why this is not just about code review

The same mechanism governs verifying a claim, confirming a fix, and checking a
report from another agent. Whenever you already know what the answer is supposed
to be, you will check for the match. Changing the reader is not enough — see
`session-discipline.md`, "Confirm a claim by a different method than produced it".
Changing the operation is the thing that works.
--- DRAFT ENDS ---
